source_text: Commendatiorem fieri putas, quod ei serviunt, ut ardentius excitetur, etiam ceterae corporis partes, sive oculi videntes ad concupiscendum, sive alia membra in osculis et amplexibus
pass_a_gloss: Commendatiorem to-become putas, that/which to-him serviunt, so-that/as ardentius excitetur, also ceterae of-the-body partes, or oculi they-see to concupiscendum, or other members in osculis and amplexibus.
pass_b_english: Augustine reports that Julian regarded desire as more commendable because other bodily parts serve to excite it: eyes seeing in order to desire, and other members in kisses and embraces.

When drunken young men, excited also by flute music as often happens, were breaking down a chaste woman’s door, Pythagoras is said to have told the flute player to play a solemn spondaic rhythm. When she did, the slowness of the measures and gravity of the song quieted their raging insolence. [Cicero, On His Own Counsels, a lost work.]
It receives consent rather than commands.
It is excited by other stimuli, or broken and quieted by music.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded. This row is Augustine's report; Pass A glosses only the Julian words recoverable here.
